{{for|the particular instance of the notion in algebraic geometry|diagonal embedding}}
[[File:Diagonal and co-diagonal.svg|right|thumb|200px]]
In [[category theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], for every [[object (category theory)|object]] <math>A</math> in every [[category (mathematics)|category]] <math>\mathcal{C}</math> where the [[product (category theory)|product]] <math>A\times A</math> exists, there exists the '''diagonal morphism'''<ref>{{harv|Carter|Crans|Elhamdadi|Saito|2008}}</ref><ref name=Faith1973>{{harv|Faith|1973}}</ref><ref name=Popescu1979>{{harv|Popescu|Popescu|1979|loc=Exercise 7.2.}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Diagonal in nlab}}</ref><ref name=Laurent2013 >{{harv|Laurent|2013}}</ref><ref name=Masakatsu1972>{{harv|Masakatsu|1972|loc=Definition 4.}}</ref>

:<math>\delta_A : A \rightarrow A \times A</math>

satisfying 

:<math>\pi_k \circ \delta_A = \operatorname{id}_A</math> for <math>k \in \{ 1,2 \},</math>

where <math>\pi_k</math> is the [[canonical projection morphism]] to the <math>k</math>-th component. The existence of this [[morphism]] is a consequence of the [[universal property]] that [[characterization (mathematics)|characterize]]s the product ([[up to]] [[isomorphism]]). The restriction to binary products here is for ease of notation; diagonal morphisms exist similarly for arbitrary products. The [[image (category theory)|image]] of a diagonal morphism in the [[category of sets]], as a [[subset]] of the [[Cartesian product]], is a [[relation (mathematics)|relation]] on the [[domain of a function|domain]], namely [[equality (mathematics)|equality]].

For [[concrete categories]], the diagonal morphism can be simply described by its action on elements <math>x</math> of the object <math>A</math>. Namely, <math>\delta_A(x) = \langle x,x \rangle</math>, the [[ordered pair]] formed from <math>x</math>. The reason for the name is that the [[Image (mathematics)|image]] of such a diagonal morphism is diagonal (whenever it makes sense), for example the image of the diagonal morphism <math>\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2</math> on the [[real line]] is given by the line that is the [[graph of a function|graph]] of the equation <math>y=x</math>. The diagonal morphism into the [[infinite product]] <math>X^\infty</math> may provide an [[Injective function|injection]] into the [[space of sequences]] valued in <math>X</math>; each element maps to the constant [[sequence]] at that element. However, most notions of sequence spaces have [[convergent series|convergence]] restrictions that the image of the diagonal map will fail to satisfy.

The dual notion of a diagonal morphism is a '''codiagonal morphism'''. For every object <math>B</math> in a category <math>\mathcal{C}</math> where the [[coproducts]] <math>B \sqcup B</math> exists, the codiagonal{{R|Popescu1979}}{{R|Faith1973}}<ref>{{harv|codiagonal in nlab}}</ref>{{R|Laurent2013}}{{R|Masakatsu1972}} is the canonical morphism

:<math>\delta_B \colon  B \sqcup B \stackrel{[Id,Id]}  \to B</math>

satisfying 

:<math>\delta_B \circ \tau_l = \operatorname{id}_B</math> for <math>l \in \{ 1,2 \}.</math>

where <math>\tau_l</math> is the injection morphism to the <math>l</math>-th component.
